Nimble is the better choice only if you want to outsource extraction to managed SERP and e-commerce APIs or its AI browser. For anyone running their own scrapers, FloppyData is the cheaper starting point, though it has less independent benchmarking.

FloppyData and Nimble sit at the two extremes of the residential proxy market. FloppyData charges a flat $1/GB on one balance for residential, mobile and datacenter traffic, aimed at budget buyers. Nimble (Nimbleway) charges premium per-GB rates and focuses on AI-driven browsing, search agents and managed data pipelines. This comparison is really about whether you need cheap IPs to run your own tools or a managed data service.

blocks.text: FloppyData in 2026: what you get

FloppyData sells proxies the way prepaid phone plans sell minutes: one flat $1/GB balance that works across residential, mobile and datacenter pools. Static residential IPs start at $1.79 each in monthly bundles (20 for $49) with unlimited bandwidth. It is one of the cheapest ways into residential traffic, but it is a newer brand with less independent benchmarking than the established names.

Strengths: Flat $1/GB on any volume; One balance across residential, mobile and datacenter; Cheap static residential bundles with unlimited bandwidth; Free cloud anti-detect browser. Weak spots: Newer brand with limited independent testing; Pool-size claims disputed by some reviewers; Mixed customer-support reviews.
Nimble in 2026: what you get

Nimbleway, now usually just called Nimble, has moved from selling proxies to selling web data. Its residential proxies still exist as an infrastructure product, but the company's focus is its AI-driven Nimble Browser, scraping APIs priced per 1,000 URLs, and managed data pipelines. Nimble does not publish a residential pool size, and its proxy product is documented for HTTP and HTTPS rather than SOCKS5. Buyers who want raw bandwidth tend to find it expensive; buyers who want finished data find it convenient.

Strengths: Strong managed APIs and an AI-driven browser; Unlimited concurrency on proxies; Credits shared across all Nimble products; Free 5,000-page API trial. Weak spots: No published pool size; HTTP/HTTPS only, no SOCKS5 on proxies; High per-GB price for raw residential traffic.
Pricing: FloppyData vs Nimble

FloppyData charges a flat $1/GB for rotating traffic, and the same balance works for residential, mobile and datacenter IPs. Static residential proxies are sold in monthly bundles from $1.79 per IP (20 IPs for $49), and static datacenter IPs from $0.79 per IP.

Nimble's plan cards list residential proxy traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go, falling through credit packages ($150 and $600 entry packages) toward $5.30/GB; its current developer documentation lists $5.30/GB for residential traffic without a commitment. Annual billing saves 15%. Its scraping APIs bill $0.90 to $1.45 per 1,000 URLs depending on rendering.

For a 10 GB month, FloppyData costs about $10 while Nimble costs about $53, so FloppyData saves around 81%. For a 100 GB month, FloppyData costs about $100 while Nimble costs about $530, so FloppyData saves around 81%. Both FloppyData and Nimble work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

FloppyData and Nimble do not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. FloppyData lists '65M+ claimed (disputed)' and Nimble lists 'Not published'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, FloppyData lists 148 (residential) countries and Nimble lists Worldwide. On targeting, FloppyData offers country and city, while Nimble offers country, state and city.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Protocol support is a real difference here. FloppyData supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, while Nimble offers HTTP, HTTPS. If your tooling needs SOCKS5, for example some anti-detect browsers, desktop apps or non-HTTP traffic, that settles it in FloppyData's favour. On sessions, FloppyData offers rotating or sticky sessions, and Nimble offers auto-rotation by default; sticky sessions available. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Nimble wins. The deciding factor for Nimble: its managed APIs remove much of the anti-bot work. The limitation on the FloppyData side: cheap, but with limited independent benchmarking.
SERP and rank tracking: Nimble. Nimble has the edge here. Why: its SERP API and search agents return structured results. How FloppyData compares: workable for light tasks.

Social media and multi-account management: FloppyData. FloppyData has the edge here. Why: cheap static residential IPs and a free anti-detect browser. How Nimble compares: no SOCKS5 and a high per-GB cost make it a poor fit for account work.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Nimble. Nimble has the edge here. Why: dedicated e-commerce data APIs. How FloppyData compares: city targeting at a flat rate.

Ad verification and geo-testing: Nimble wins. The deciding factor for Nimble: good geo targeting but no published pool data. The limitation on the FloppyData side: limited targeting depth and published data.
Tight budgets: FloppyData wins. The deciding factor for FloppyData: a flat $1/GB on any volume. The limitation on the Nimble side: per-GB rates are among the highest here.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. FloppyData: No free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations. Nimble: Free trial of 5,000 web pages on its APIs. Verification and payment rules differ too. FloppyData: Light. Nimble: Sales-led onboarding for data-services plans. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test FloppyData and Nimble before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle FloppyData vs Nimble faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (FloppyData: no free trial; free browser extension for testing a few locations; Nimble: free trial of 5,000 web pages on its APIs).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, FloppyData comes out ahead in 2, Nimble in 4, and 0 are ties. That makes Nimble the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: FloppyData is strongest for small budgets and experiments, while Nimble is strongest for teams that want structured data rather than raw IPs. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
